context: A beam of electrons with kinetic energy K=1\unit{keV} is diffracted as it passes through a polycrystalline metal foil. The metal has a cubic crystal structure with interplanar spacing d=1\unit{\AA}. Use de Broglie theory for matter waves and Bragg's law for diffraction. Use the following symbols throughout: m for the electron mass, q for the magnitude of the electron charge, h for Planck's constant, c for the speed of light, K for the electron kinetic energy, p for the electron momentum, \lambda for the electron de Broglie wavelength, d for the lattice plane spacing, n for the diffraction order, and \theta for the Bragg angle. 20'

subquestions.subproblem: calculate the wavelength of the electrons,
subquestions.solution:
The electron wavelength is given by
$$
\lambda = \frac{h}{p}
$$
with the momentum determined by the kinetic energy
$$
\frac{p^2}{2m} = K
$$
so that
$$
p = \sqrt{2mK}
$$
Therefore
$$
\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}
$$
For K=1\unit{keV}, this gives the numerical estimate
$$
\lambda \approx 0.39\unit{\AA}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the electron de Broglie wavelength \lambda as a numerical value in angstroms (\AA). Report your result to 2 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: calculate the Bragg angle for the first order diffraction maximum.
subquestions.solution:
Bragg's condition is
$$
2d \sin \theta = n \lambda
$$
For the first order maximum
$$
n = 1
$$
so
$$
\sin \theta = \frac{\lambda}{2d}
$$
With d=1\unit{\AA} and \lambda \approx 0.39\unit{\AA}, one finds
$$
\sin \theta \approx 0.195
$$
Hence
$$
\theta \approx 11.18\unit{^\circ}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the Bragg angle \theta for the first-order (n=1) diffraction maximum as a numerical value in degrees. Report your result to 4 significant figures.

context: Estimate, to within 10%, the wavelength λ of the most energetic line in the characteristic X-ray spectrum of copper. Let Z denote the atomic number of copper with Z=29. Model the line as an electron transition from the N shell (principal quantum number n=4) to a vacancy in the K shell (n=1), and approximate the screening of the K shell by using an effective nuclear charge Z_eff=Z-1 in a hydrogenic formula. Let R denote the Rydberg constant. Report λ in meters; you may also give it in ångströms. All symbols used in the solution are defined here.
solution:
The ground-state electron configuration of copper (Z=29) is 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^{10} 4s^1. The most energetic prominent characteristic X-ray line is modeled as the transition from n=4 to n=1, with K-shell screening approximated by Z-1. Using the screened hydrogenic relation for the wavenumber, we write
$$
\frac{1}{\lambda} = R (Z-1)^2 \left( \frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{4^2} \right)
$$
where R is the Rydberg constant
$$
R = 1.09678\times 10^7 \unit{m^{-1}}
$$
Substituting Z=29 gives the wavelength
$$
\lambda = 1.24\times 10^{-10} \unit{m}
$$
Equivalently
$$
\lambda = 1.24 \unit{\AA}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the wavelength λ as a numerical value. Report λ in meters; you may also give it in ångströms. Use three significant figures.

context: Give an approximate incident energy for which a crystal lattice would make a good diffraction grating for photons. subquestions.subproblem: photons.
subquestions.solution:
If the incident photons can just be diffracted by a crystal lattice, take the wavelength to be of order the lattice spacing
$$
\lambda \approx 10^{-10} \unit{m}
$$
Using E = hν and ν = c/λ
$$
E = h \nu
$$
$$
\nu = \frac{c}{\lambda}
$$
$$
E = \frac{h c}{\lambda}
$$
Numerically
$$
E = \frac{\left(6.624 \times 10^{-34} \unit{J s}\right) \left(3 \times 10^{8} \unit{m/s}\right)}{10^{-10} \unit{m}}
$$
$$
E = 1.98 \times 10^{-15} \unit{J}
$$
$$
E = 12420 \unit{eV}
$$

context: X-rays are reflected from a crystal by Bragg reflection. Consider a crystal with a known structure; for definiteness, take a simple cubic primitive cell with lattice spacing d (results for other structures differ by a factor of order unity). First-order reflection is used with n=1. The angle θ that the incident and reflected rays each make with the reflecting crystal plane is θ=6 degrees, measured with an rms angular uncertainty of 3.4 minutes of arc. The mass density ρ of the crystal is measured with an rms fractional uncertainty of 3 parts in 10^4. Let λ be the X-ray wavelength. Let σ_x denote the rms uncertainty in x. The molar mass is M and Avogadro's number is N_0. Using these definitions, determine the rms fractional uncertainty σ_λ/λ in the wavelength.
solution:
For first-order reflection, Bragg's law gives
$$
2 d \sin \theta = \lambda
$$
Differentiating gives
$$
\left| \frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda} \right| = \left| \frac{\Delta d}{d} \right| + \cot \theta \left| \Delta \theta \right|
$$
The unit cell volume for a simple cubic lattice is
$$
d^3 = \frac{M}{\rho N_0}
$$
Differentiating yields
$$
\left| \frac{\Delta d}{d} \right| = \frac{1}{3} \left| \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \right|
$$
Combining the results gives
$$
\left| \frac{\Delta \lambda}{\lambda} \right| = \frac{1}{3} \left| \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \right| + \cot \theta \left| \Delta \theta \right|
$$
Assuming independent uncertainties, the rms fractional uncertainty is
$$
\frac{\sigma_\lambda}{\lambda} = \left[ \left( \frac{1}{3} \frac{\sigma_\rho}{\rho} \right)^2 + \left( \sigma_\theta \cot \theta \right)^2 \right]^{1/2}
$$
With the given values
$$
\frac{\sigma_\rho}{\rho} = 3 \times 10^{-4}
$$
Convert the angles to radians for SI consistency
$$
\theta = \frac{\pi}{30} \unit{rad}
$$
$$
\sigma_\theta = \frac{17 \pi}{54000} \unit{rad}
$$
Using the small-angle approximation for the product and noting cancellation in the ratio
$$
\sigma_\theta \cot \theta \approx \frac{\sigma_\theta}{\theta}
$$
Numerically
$$
\frac{\sigma_\theta}{\theta} = \frac{3.4}{60 \times 6}
$$
Hence
$$
\sigma_\theta \cot \theta = 9.4 \times 10^{-3}
$$
Therefore
$$
\frac{\sigma_\lambda}{\lambda} = \sqrt{10^{-8} + \left( 9.4 \times 10^{-3} \right)^2}
$$
$$
\frac{\sigma_\lambda}{\lambda} = 9.4 \times 10^{-3}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the rms fractional uncertainty σ_λ/λ as a numerical value. Report your result to 2 significant figures.

context: Estimate the pressure p needed to compress an isothermal elastic solid to several times its normal density. Let v be the volume at pressure p and temperature T, and v_0 the initial volume at normal density. Let rho be the density at pressure p and rho_0 the normal density. Define the bulk modulus K by K = - v (∂p/∂v)_T and assume K is constant. Define the compression factor alpha by rho = alpha rho_0 with alpha > 1. Use K ≈ 10^8 millibar (mb), equivalently K ≈ 10^{10} pascal (Pa). Compute p for the case alpha = 10. Use E_k for kinetic energy, E_p for potential energy, E for total energy, M for the mass of the central body, m for the mass of the satellite, and R for the radius of the orbit only if needed in other contexts; they are not used in this problem
solution:
To compress isothermally an elastic solid of volume v by dv, the pressure increment dp required is defined through the bulk modulus K by
$$
K = - v \frac{\partial p}{\partial v}
$$
Assuming K is constant, integrating from v_0 to v gives
$$
p = - \int_{v_0}^{v} K \frac{dv}{v}
$$
Evaluating the integral yields
$$
p = K \ln \frac{v_0}{v}
$$
For compression to alpha times the normal density, the volume and density ratios satisfy
$$
\frac{v_0}{v} = \frac{\rho}{\rho_0}
$$
and by definition of alpha,
$$
\frac{\rho}{\rho_0} = \alpha
$$
Hence the required pressure is
$$
p = K \ln \alpha
$$
For typical solids, take
$$
K = 10^8 \unit{mb}
$$
which is equivalently
$$
K = 10^{10} \unit{Pa}
$$
For alpha = 10,
$$
p = 10^8 \ln 10 \unit{mb}
$$
Numerically,
$$
p = 2.3 \times 10^8 \unit{mb}
$$
In SI units,
$$
p = 2.3 \times 10^{10} \unit{Pa}
$$
Expressed approximately in atmospheres,
$$
p = 2.3 \times 10^5 \unit{atm}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the required pressure p in pascals (Pa) as a numerical value. Round your result to 2 significant figures.

context: Consider a one-dimensional line of 2N ions with alternating charges ±q. Let R denote the nearest-neighbor separation. The interaction between nearest neighbors consists of the usual Coulomb potential and an additional short-range repulsive potential A/R^n, where A>0 and n>1 are constants. Neglect surface effects, and define the lattice energy U(R) of the entire chain of 2N ions accordingly. Let a denote the Madelung constant of the one-dimensional alternating chain, R_0 the equilibrium nearest-neighbor separation that minimizes U(R), and W the work done by applied forces when compressing the lattice from R_0 to R=R_0(1−δ), with 0<δ≪1 the small fractional compression. The total length of the crystal is approximately 2 N R_0. For a one-dimensional alternating chain, the Madelung constant is a=2 ln 2.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the equilibrium separation R_0 for such a system and evaluate the equilibrium energy U(R_0).
subquestions.solution:
Neglecting surface effects, the lattice energy is
$$U(R)=N\left(-\frac{a q^2}{R}+\frac{A}{R^n}\right)$$
At equilibrium, U(R) is minimized, so
$$\frac{dU}{dR}\bigg|_{R=R_0}=0$$
Solving for the equilibrium separation gives
$$R_0=\left(\frac{nA}{a q^2}\right)^{\frac{1}{n-1}}$$
From the equilibrium condition one has
$$\frac{A}{R_0^{n-1}}=\frac{a q^2}{n}$$
Therefore
$$U(R_0)=-\frac{N}{R_0}\left(a q^2-\frac{A}{R_0^{n-1}}\right)$$
and hence
$$U(R_0)=-\frac{N a q^2}{R_0}\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)$$
For a one-dimensional chain,
$$a=2\ln 2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include two expressions and be written explicitly as: (1) R_0 = ... using only A, a, q, n; and (2) U(R_0) = ... using only N, a, q, n, R_0.

subquestions.subproblem: Let the crystal be compressed so that R_0 → R_0(1−δ). Calculate the work done in compressing a unit length of the crystal to order δ^2.
subquestions.solution:
When the crystal is compressed to R=R_0(1-\delta), the increase in lattice energy is
$$U(R)-U(R_0)=N\left[-a q^2\left(\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{R_0}\right)+A\left(\frac{1}{R^n}-\frac{1}{R_0^n}\right)\right]$$
This equals the work W done by the applied forces
$$W=U(R)-U(R_0)$$
Using R=R_0(1-\delta), expand to order \delta^2:
$$\frac{R_0}{R}-1=(1-\delta)^{-1}-1$$
$$\frac{R_0}{R}-1\approx\delta+\delta^2$$
$$(\frac{R_0}{R})^n-1=(1-\delta)^{-n}-1$$
$$(\frac{R_0}{R})^n-1\approx n\delta+\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\delta^2$$
Keeping terms up to order \delta^2 gives
$$W\approx\frac{N a q^2}{2 R_0}(n-1)\delta^2$$
The total length is approximately L=2 N R_0, so the work per unit length is
$$\frac{W}{2 N R_0}=\frac{a q^2}{4 R_0^2}(n-1)\delta^2$$
For the one-dimensional chain with a=2\ln 2,
$$\frac{W}{2 N R_0}=\frac{q^2}{R_0^2}\frac{\ln 2}{2}(n-1)\delta^2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form W/(2 N R_0) = ... up to and including terms of order δ^2, and your response should be written with a, q, R_0, n, δ only.

context: An ideal two-dimensional monatomic crystal has atoms of mass m on a square lattice with lattice constant a. Equilibrium lattice sites are labeled by integers r,s=1,2,...,N and have position R=(r a,s a). The displacement of the atom at site (r,s) is denoted by the components (x_{rs},y_{rs}), so its instantaneous position is given by the vector R_{rs}=(r a+x_{rs},s a+y_{rs}). In the harmonic approximation the potential energy is taken as a sum over nearest neighbors with spring constants k_1 and k_2, where k_1 couples x-displacements along the r-direction and y-displacements along the s-direction, while k_2 couples x-displacements along the s-direction and y-displacements along the r-direction. The potential is therefore V(x_{rs},y_{rs})=sum_{r,s}{ k_1[(x_{r+1,s}-x_{rs})^2+(y_{r,s+1}-y_{rs})^2] + k_2[(x_{r,s+1}-x_{rs})^2+(y_{r+1,s}-y_{rs})^2] }. The wavevector is q=(q_x,q_y) within the first Brillouin zone of the square lattice, with -\pi/a \le q_x,q_y \le \pi/a. In what follows, \omega_{q\lambda} denotes the phonon angular frequency for wavevector q in branch \lambda\in\{1,2\}. The unit vectors e_x and e_y point along the Cartesian x and y axes, respectively. Consider the case k_2=\frac{1}{10}k_1.

subquestions.subproblem: Determine the general phonon dispersion relation \omega_{q\lambda} throughout the Brillouin zone.
subquestions.solution: Newton's second law for the atom at site (r,s) reads $$m \ddot R_{rs} = - \nabla_{rs} V$$ where the site gradient operator is $$\nabla_{rs} = e_x \frac{\partial}{\partial x_{rs}} + e_y \frac{\partial}{\partial y_{rs}}$$ Seek plane-wave solutions with time dependence e^{-i \omega t} and spatial phase q\cdot R, using the component ansatz $$x_{rs} = A_x e^{i[(q_x r + q_y s)a - \omega t]}$$ $$y_{rs} = A_y e^{i[(q_x r + q_y s)a - \omega t]}$$ From the equation of motion for x_{rs} one obtains $$- m \omega^2 x_{rs} = 2 k_1 (e^{i q_x a} + e^{- i q_x a} - 2) x_{rs} + 2 k_2 (e^{i q_y a} + e^{- i q_y a} - 2) x_{rs}$$ which gives $$\omega^2 = \frac{4 k_1}{m} [1 - \cos(q_x a)] + \frac{4 k_2}{m} [1 - \cos(q_y a)]$$ Using the half-angle identity this can be written as $$\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 \bigg[ \sin^2\Big(\frac{q_x a}{2}\Big) + \frac{k_2}{k_1} \sin^2\Big(\frac{q_y a}{2}\Big) \bigg]$$ where $$\omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{8 k_1}{m}}$$ By symmetry, the y_{rs} equation yields the second branch with q_x and q_y interchanged. Therefore, for general k_2/k_1 the two branches are $$\omega_{q1} = \omega_0 \bigg[ \sin^2\Big(\frac{q_x a}{2}\Big) + \frac{k_2}{k_1} \sin^2\Big(\frac{q_y a}{2}\Big) \bigg]^{1/2}$$ $$\omega_{q2} = \omega_0 \bigg[ \sin^2\Big(\frac{q_y a}{2}\Big) + \frac{k_2}{k_1} \sin^2\Big(\frac{q_x a}{2}\Big) \bigg]^{1/2}$$ For the specified case k_2 = \frac{1}{10} k_1 these become $$\omega_{q1} = \omega_0 \bigg[ \sin^2\Big(\frac{q_x a}{2}\Big) + \frac{1}{10} \sin^2\Big(\frac{q_y a}{2}\Big) \bigg]^{1/2}$$ $$\omega_{q2} = \omega_0 \bigg[ \sin^2\Big(\frac{q_y a}{2}\Big) + \frac{1}{10} \sin^2\Big(\frac{q_x a}{2}\Big) \bigg]^{1/2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of two explicit formulas, \u03c9_{q1}(q_x,q_y) = ... and \u03c9_{q2}(q_x,q_y) = ..., and your response should be written only with the variables q_x, q_y, a, k_1, k_2, and m (do not introduce additional parameters).

subquestions.subproblem: Sketch \omega_{q\lambda} as a function of q for the line q=(\xi,0) with 0 \le \xi \le \pi/a.
subquestions.solution: Along this line the wavevector components are $$q_x = \xi$$ $$q_y = 0$$ Hence the two branches reduce to $$\omega_{q1} = \omega_0 \bigg| \sin\Big(\frac{\xi a}{2}\Big) \bigg|$$ $$\omega_{q2} = \omega_0 \sqrt{\frac{1}{10}} \bigg| \sin\Big(\frac{\xi a}{2}\Big) \bigg|$$ for $$0 \le \xi \le \frac{\pi}{a}$$ The resulting curves are sinusoidal with different amplitudes and are illustrated in Fig. 1.5

context: Consider a two-dimensional square lattice with lattice constant a and one atom of mass m at each lattice point. Atoms interact only with their nearest neighbors via a harmonic interatomic force constant K. The acoustic phonon dispersion relation is taken to be $$\omega_q=\sqrt{\frac{4K}{m}}\sin\left(\frac{qa}{2}\right)$$ where q=|q| is the magnitude of the wavevector. In the long-wavelength limit, define the sound speed v by v=\omega_q/q. The system occupies a square of linear size L and area S=L^2. There are two acoustic polarizations. Define N(\omega) as the number of normal modes with angular frequency less than \omega, and D(\omega)=dN/d\omega as the density of phonon states per unit angular-frequency interval. Let k_B be the Boltzmann constant, \hbar the reduced Planck constant, and T the absolute temperature. Define the Debye cutoff frequency \omega_D by the condition that the total number of acoustic modes equals 2N, where N is the number of atoms in the lattice.

subquestions.subproblem: In the long-wavelength limit, obtain the density of phonon states D(\omega)=dN/d\omega, i.e., the number of lattice-vibration modes per frequency interval d\omega:
subquestions.solution: In the long-wavelength limit q\to 0, use \sin(qa/2)\approx qa/2 to obtain $$\omega_q\approx\sqrt{\frac{K}{m}}\,a\,q$$ The sound speed is defined by $$v=\frac{\omega_q}{q}$$ Hence $$v=\sqrt{\frac{K}{m}}\,a$$ In the Debye model, the number of normal modes with wavevectors of magnitude not exceeding q is $$N(q)=2\,\frac{\pi q^2}{(2\pi/L)^2}$$ Therefore $$N(q)=\frac{L^2 q^2}{2\pi}$$ Using q=\omega/v, we obtain $$N(\omega)=\frac{S}{2\pi}\frac{\omega^2}{v^2}$$ The density of states is $$D(\omega)=\frac{dN}{d\omega}$$ Therefore $$D(\omega)=\frac{S\omega}{\pi v^2}$$ Using v^2=\frac{K}{m}a^2, we find $$D(\omega)=\frac{S m\omega}{\pi a^2 K}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of D(ω) = ..., and your response should be written with S, ω, v only.

subquestions.subproblem: At high temperature (k_B T \gg \hbar \omega), find the mean square displacement of an atom from its equilibrium position, and comment on the stability of two-dimensional crystals.
subquestions.solution: The total internal energy of the lattice is $$U=\int_0^{\omega_D}\frac{\hbar\omega}{e^{\hbar\omega/(k_B T)}-1}D(\omega) d\omega$$ In the high-temperature limit \hbar\omega\ll k_B T, we use $$\frac{\hbar\omega}{e^{\hbar\omega/(k_B T)}-1}\approx k_B T$$ Hence $$U\approx\int_0^{\omega_D}k_B T D(\omega) d\omega$$ With D(\omega)=S\omega/(\pi v^2), we obtain $$U=\frac{S k_B T}{\pi v^2}\int_0^{\omega_D}\omega d\omega$$ Therefore $$U=\frac{S k_B T}{2\pi v^2}\omega_D^2$$ The Debye cutoff is fixed by mode counting at \omega_D as $$N(\omega_D)=\frac{S}{2\pi}\frac{\omega_D^2}{v^2}$$ The total number of acoustic modes equals twice the number of atoms as $$2N=N(\omega_D)$$ Hence $$\omega_D^2=\frac{4\pi N v^2}{S}$$ Substituting gives $$U=2 N k_B T$$ By equipartition, the average potential energy equals the average kinetic energy and thus equals U/2, so $$E_{pot}=\frac{U}{2}$$ If \langle r^2\rangle is the mean square displacement of an atom, the total potential energy can be written as $$E_{pot}=\frac{N}{2}K\langle r^2\rangle$$ Equating these yields $$\frac{N}{2}K\langle r^2\rangle=N k_B T$$ Therefore $$\langle r^2\rangle=\frac{2 k_B T}{K}$$ Since \langle r^2\rangle\propto T, as T increases sufficiently, \sqrt{\langle r^2\rangle} can exceed the lattice constant a, indicating that a two-dimensional lattice is unstable at high temperatures
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer must consist of two parts presented together: (1) an algebraic expression in the form of ⟨r²⟩ = ..., written only with k_B, T, K; and (2) a separate one-sentence statement in the exact form: 'The two-dimensional crystal is stable/unstable at high temperature.'

context: Assume ideal-gas behavior where appropriate. Let R be the universal gas constant, k_B the Boltzmann constant, and N the Avogadro number, with R = N k_B. Let f denote the number of quadratic degrees of freedom per molecule. For part (c), consider one mole of a monatomic crystalline solid of volume V containing N atoms. Let v_0 be the speed of sound in the crystal. Let ω denote angular frequency, D(ω) the density of normal modes, and ω_m the Debye cutoff frequency. Define the reduced Planck constant ħ, temperature T, the internal energy U, and the molar specific heat at constant volume C_v. Introduce the dimensionless variable x = ħ ω/(k_B T), with upper limit x_m = ħ ω_m/(k_B T), and the Debye temperature Θ = ħ ω_m/k_B. Define the function F(y) by F(y) = y^3 ∫_0^{1/y} e^x x^4/(e^x - 1)^2 dx, so that C_v can be written as C_v = 9 N k_B F(T/Θ).

subquestions.subproblem: What is the specific heat (per mole) of a monatomic gas at constant volume?
subquestions.solution:
For a monatomic ideal gas, the number of quadratic degrees of freedom is
$$f = 3$$
By equipartition, the molar specific heat at constant volume is
$$C_v = \frac{3}{2} R$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of 'C_v = ...', and your response should use only the symbol R.

subquestions.subproblem: What is its specific heat (per mole) at constant volume for a diatomic gas? Explain.
subquestions.solution:
For an ideal diatomic gas with translational and rotational modes active and vibrational modes frozen, the number of quadratic degrees of freedom is
$$f = 5$$
Hence the molar specific heat at constant volume is
$$C_v = \frac{5}{2} R$$
For ideal gases under these assumptions, the molar specific heat is independent of temperature over the range where the assumed degrees of freedom are active.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of 'C_v = ...', and your response should use only the symbol R.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the specific heat of a monatomic crystalline solid?
subquestions.solution:
Consider one mole of a monatomic crystalline solid of volume V containing N atoms. There are 3N normal modes of vibration. The number of modes with frequencies in the range ω to ω + dω is
$$D(\omega) d\omega = \frac{3 V \omega^2 d\omega}{2 \pi^2 v_0^3}$$
The Debye cutoff frequency satisfies
$$\omega_m = \left( \frac{6 \pi^2 N}{V} \right)^{1/3} v_0$$
The average energy of an oscillator of frequency ω is
$$\frac{\hbar \omega}{e^{\hbar \omega/(k_B T)} - 1}$$
The total internal energy is
$$U = \int_0^{\omega_m} \frac{\hbar \omega}{e^{\hbar \omega/(k_B T)} - 1} D(\omega) d\omega$$
Substituting D(ω) gives
$$U = \frac{3 V \hbar}{2 \pi^2 v_0^3} \int_0^{\omega_m} \frac{\omega^3}{e^{\hbar \omega/(k_B T)} - 1} d\omega$$
The molar specific heat at constant volume is
$$C_v = \left( \frac{\partial U}{\partial T} \right)_V$$
With the substitution
$$x = \frac{\hbar \omega}{k_B T}$$
and upper limit
$$x_m = \frac{\hbar \omega_m}{k_B T}$$
we obtain
$$C_v = \frac{3 V k_B}{2 \pi^2} \left( \frac{T k_B}{\hbar v_0} \right)^3 \int_0^{x_m} \frac{e^x x^4}{(e^x - 1)^2} dx$$
Define the Debye temperature
$$\Theta = \frac{\hbar \omega_m}{k_B}$$
Then
$$C_v = 9 N k_B \left( \frac{T}{\Theta} \right)^3 \int_0^{\Theta/T} \frac{e^x x^4}{(e^x - 1)^2} dx$$
Introduce the function
$$F\!\left( \frac{T}{\Theta} \right) = \left( \frac{T}{\Theta} \right)^3 \int_0^{\Theta/T} \frac{e^x x^4}{(e^x - 1)^2} dx$$
so that
$$C_v = 9 N k_B F\!\left( \frac{T}{\Theta} \right)$$
In the high-temperature limit
$$T \gg \Theta$$
we have for small x
$$\frac{e^x x^4}{(e^x - 1)^2} \approx x^2$$
Thus
$$F\!\left( \frac{T}{\Theta} \right) \approx \frac{1}{3}$$
which gives
$$C_v \approx 3 N k_B$$
Using R = N k_B, this is
$$C_v \approx 3 R$$
In the low-temperature limit
$$T \ll \Theta$$
we may take the upper limit to infinity, yielding

context: Use the Debye model to calculate the low-temperature heat capacity at constant volume C_v of a one-dimensional monatomic lattice. The lattice has N atoms, length L, and lattice spacing a with L = N a. The acoustic phonon branch has linear dispersion omega = v |k| with sound speed v. The Debye temperature Theta_D is defined by Theta_D = hbar pi v / (k_B a), where hbar is the reduced Planck constant and k_B is Boltzmann's constant. Work in the regime T << Theta_D. The Debye cutoff frequency omega_D is chosen by mode counting so that the total number of modes equals N. Numerical constants in the form of integrals need not be evaluated.
solution:
In the Debye model, the one-dimensional density of states is
$$
\rho(\omega) = \frac{L}{\pi v}
$$

The average energy per mode of frequency omega at temperature T is
$$
\epsilon(\omega,T) = \frac{\hbar \omega}{e^{\hbar \omega/(k_B T)} - 1}
$$

The internal energy is
$$
U = \int_0^{\omega_D} \rho(\omega) \epsilon(\omega,T) d\omega
$$

The Debye cutoff omega_D is fixed by mode counting
$$
\int_0^{\omega_D} \rho(\omega) d\omega = N
$$

Hence
$$
\omega_D = \frac{\pi N v}{L}
$$

Using L = N a gives
$$
N = \frac{L}{a}
$$

Therefore
$$
\omega_D = \frac{\pi v}{a}
$$

By definition of the Debye temperature
$$
\Theta_D = \frac{\hbar \omega_D}{k_B}
$$

Equivalently
$$
\omega_D = \frac{k_B \Theta_D}{\hbar}
$$

The heat capacity at constant volume is
$$
C_v = \frac{\partial U}{\partial T}
$$

Introduce the dimensionless variable
$$
x = \frac{\hbar \omega}{k_B T}
$$

Then
$$
C_v = N k_B \frac{T}{\Theta_D} \int_0^{\Theta_D/T} \frac{x^2 e^x}{(e^x - 1)^2} dx
$$

In the low-temperature limit
$$
T \ll \Theta_D
$$

we have
$$
\frac{\Theta_D}{T} \approx \infty
$$

and the integral evaluates to
$$
\int_0^{\infty} \frac{x^2 e^x}{(e^x - 1)^2} dx = \frac{\pi^2}{3}
$$

Thus
$$
C_v = \frac{\pi^2}{3} N k_B \frac{T}{\Theta_D}
$$

Using \Theta_D = \hbar \pi v / (k_B a) gives
$$
C_v = \frac{\pi k_B^2 N a}{3 \hbar v} T
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of C_v = ..., and your response should be written with N, k_B, T, and Theta_D only.

context: Graphite has a layered crystal structure in which the coupling between the carbon atoms in different layers is much weaker than the coupling between atoms within the same layer. Experimentally it is found that the specific heat at constant volume satisfies C_v ∝ T^2 at low temperatures. Using Debye theory adapted to such a layered structure, explain this behavior. Use the following definitions and assumptions: T is the absolute temperature, v indicates that derivatives are taken at constant volume, C_v is the specific heat at constant volume defined by C_v=(∂E/∂T)_v, ρ(ω) is the phonon density of states of the whole crystal as a function of angular frequency ω, A is a positive normalization constant defined by ρ(ω)=Aω for the layered crystal and determined by the Debye cutoff normalization, N is the number of atoms in the crystal, ω_D is the Debye cutoff angular frequency, Θ_D is the Debye temperature defined by Θ_D=ℏω_D/k_B, E is the total internal energy of the lattice, k_B is the Boltzmann constant, ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, x is the dimensionless integration variable defined by x=ℏω/(k_B T). Assume three acoustic polarizations per wavevector.
solution:
In the Debye model for a two-dimensional lattice, the phonon density of states is proportional to ω. For a layered crystal with very weak interlayer coupling, the total density of states can be approximated by the sum over independent layers, so it remains proportional to ω. Hence we write
$$
\rho(\omega)=A\omega
$$
The normalization with three polarizations gives
$$
\int_0^{\omega_D}\rho(\omega)d\omega=3N
$$
which yields
$$
A=\frac{6N}{\omega_D^2}
$$
The total internal energy of the lattice is
$$
E=\int_0^{\omega_D}\frac{\hbar\omega}{e^{\hbar\omega/k_B T}-1}\rho(\omega)d\omega
$$
After substituting ρ(ω)=Aω we obtain
$$
E=A\int_0^{\omega_D}\frac{\hbar\omega^2}{e^{\hbar\omega/k_B T}-1}d\omega
$$
Introduce the dimensionless variable
$$
x=\frac{\hbar\omega}{k_B T}
$$
and the Debye temperature
$$
\Theta_D=\frac{\hbar\omega_D}{k_B}
$$
The specific heat at constant volume is
$$
C_v=\frac{\partial E}{\partial T}
$$
Evaluating the derivative gives
$$
C_v=A k_B\left(\frac{k_B T}{\hbar}\right)^2\int_0^{\Theta_D/T}\frac{x^3 e^x}{(e^x-1)^2}dx
$$
In the low-temperature limit we have
$$
T\ll\Theta_D
$$
so that
$$
\int_0^{\Theta_D/T}\frac{x^3 e^x}{(e^x-1)^2}dx\approx\int_0^{\infty}\frac{x^3 e^x}{(e^x-1)^2}dx
$$
which is a T-independent constant. Therefore
$$
C_v\propto T^2
$$
This shows that Debye theory adapted to a layered crystal with weak interlayer coupling predicts C_v ∝ T^2 at low temperatures, in agreement with experiment.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as a proportionality relation of the form 'C_v ∝ T^{...}', and your response should use only the symbols C_v and T.

context: Mechanism and estimate problem for thermal conductivity in crystalline electrical insulators. In a crystalline, insulating solid at temperature T, heat is carried by phonons. Under a temperature gradient, phonons transport energy from the hot end to the cold end. Phonon-phonon interactions include normal and umklapp processes; umklapp processes dominate thermal resistance at room temperature and determine the effective mean free path. The thermal conductivity k of an electrical insulator can be modeled by the kinetic expression. Use the following definitions for variables: k is the thermal conductivity, c is the heat capacity per unit volume, v is the average phonon group velocity (of order the speed of sound), l is the phonon mean free path relevant to umklapp scattering, C_v is the molar heat capacity, and V is the molar volume. The relation between c, C_v, and V is c = C_v/V. Using representative room-temperature data for a typical ionic crystal (take NaCl as an example), estimate k.
solution:
Phonons, the quanta of lattice vibrations, mediate heat transport in crystalline insulators. A temperature gradient creates a nonequilibrium phonon population with higher population and energy at the hot end. As phonons propagate, they transfer energy toward the cold end. Due to lattice anharmonicity, phonons scatter via normal and umklapp processes; umklapp processes dominate thermal resistance at room temperature, driving the phonon distribution toward local equilibrium and setting the effective mean free path that appears in the kinetic formula.

The kinetic expression for the thermal conductivity is
$$
k = \frac{1}{3} c v l
$$
with c = C_v/V. For NaCl at room temperature, take the following representative values with physical justifications: C_v is of order a few times R per mole of the solid and we use
$$
C_v = 25 \unit{J mol^{-1} K^{-1}}
$$
The characteristic phonon speed is of order the speed of sound, taken as
$$
v = 6 \times 10^{4} \unit{m s^{-1}}
$$
The umklapp-limited phonon mean free path is estimated as
$$
l = 2.3 \times 10^{-9} \unit{m}
$$
The molar volume is
$$
V = 27 \times 10^{-6} \unit{m^{3} mol^{-1}}
$$
Hence the heat capacity per unit volume is
$$
c = \frac{C_v}{V}
$$
The resulting thermal conductivity is
$$
k = \frac{1}{3} \left(\frac{C_v}{V}\right) v l
$$
Numerically, this gives
$$
k = 43 \unit{W m^{-1} K^{-1}}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the thermal conductivity as a numerical value written in the form 'k = ...' with SI units of W m^{-1} K^{-1}. Report your result to 2 significant figures.

context: A material of mass density rho has a face-centered cubic lattice with cube edge length a_0 and an Einstein temperature theta_E. In the high-temperature limit T > theta_E, express the atomic mean square displacement along the x direction, denoted by overline{M_x^2}, in terms of rho, a_0, and theta_E, plus necessary physical constants. Definitions: T is the absolute temperature, M_x is the instantaneous displacement of an atom from its equilibrium position along x, and overline{M_x^2} is the thermal average at temperature T of M_x^2. Let m be the mass of one atom, omega_E the Einstein angular frequency, k_B the Boltzmann constant, and hbar the reduced Planck constant. In a face-centered cubic lattice there are four atoms per conventional cubic cell, so the volume per atom is a_0^3 / 4.
solution:
For an fcc lattice, the density relates to the atomic mass m by
$$
\rho = \frac{4 m}{a_0^3}
$$
The Einstein angular frequency satisfies
$$
\hbar \omega_E = k_B \theta_E
$$
For a one-dimensional quantum harmonic oscillator in the nth eigenstate, the coordinate mean square is
$$
\overline{M_x^2}_n = \frac{n + \frac{1}{2}}{m \omega_E} \hbar
$$
Thermal averaging with Boltzmann weights at temperature T gives
$$
\overline{M_x^2} = \frac{\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \overline{M_x^2}_n e^{-(n+\frac{1}{2}) \hbar \omega_E /(k_B T)}}{\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} e^{-(n+\frac{1}{2}) \hbar \omega_E /(k_B T)}}
$$
Evaluating the sums yields
$$
\overline{M_x^2} = \frac{\hbar}{m \omega_E} \left( \frac{1}{e^{\hbar \omega_E /(k_B T)} - 1} + \frac{1}{2} \right)
$$
Using
$$
m = \frac{a_0^3 \rho}{4}
$$
and
$$
\omega_E = \frac{k_B \theta_E}{\hbar}
$$
we obtain
$$
\overline{M_x^2} = \frac{4 \hbar^2}{k_B \theta_E a_0^3 \rho} \left( \frac{1}{e^{\theta_E / T} - 1} + \frac{1}{2} \right)
$$
In the high-temperature limit T \gg \theta_E, use
$$
\frac{1}{e^{\theta_E / T} - 1} + \frac{1}{2} \approx \frac{T}{\theta_E}
$$
which gives
$$
\overline{M_x^2} \approx \frac{4 \hbar^2 T}{k_B \theta_E^2 a_0^3 \rho}
$$

context: Neutron diffraction may be used to measure the dispersion relation omega versus the excitation wave vector in a crystalline solid. Assume the crystal symmetry (and therefore the reciprocal lattice) is known. Let M be the neutron mass and \hbar the reduced Planck constant. Let k and k' be the incident and scattered neutron wave vectors, with corresponding momenta p and p'. Let q denote the excitation (phonon) wave vector and omega(q) its angular frequency. Let G be a reciprocal lattice vector. Write the energy and momentum conservation laws for inelastic neutron diffraction involving excitation creation (+) or absorption (−), and then indicate which experimental parameters must be measured in order to obtain omega as a function of q.
solution:
The neutron momentum-wave vector relations are

$$
p=\hbar k
$$

$$
p'=\hbar k'
$$

The neutron kinetic energies are

$$
E=\frac{p^2}{2M}
$$

$$
E'=\frac{p'^2}{2M}
$$

Energy conservation for excitation creation (+) or absorption (−) is

$$
E=E'\pm\hbar\omega(q)
$$

Equivalently, in terms of k and k',

$$
\frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2M}=\frac{\hbar^2 k'^2}{2M}\pm\hbar\omega(q)
$$

Momentum conservation is

$$
\hbar k=\hbar k'\pm\hbar q-\hbar G
$$

To obtain \omega as a function of q, measure the energy difference between the incident and scattered neutrons as a function of the scattering direction k-k', using the known reciprocal lattice to identify G and thereby determine q from the measured k and k'

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the mixing entropy of the alloy. Assume that N = N_A + N_B >> 1.
subquestions.solution:
The mixing entropy is
$$S = k_B 
\ln \Omega$$
where
$$\Omega = \frac{N!}{N_A! N_B!}$$
Using Stirling's formula
$$\ln N! \approx N \ln N$$
we have
$$\ln \Omega \approx N_A \ln \left(1 + \frac{N_B}{N_A}\right) + N_B \ln \left(1 + \frac{N_A}{N_B}\right)$$
and hence
$$S = k_B N_A \ln \left(1 + \frac{N_B}{N_A}\right) + k_B N_B \ln \left(1 + \frac{N_A}{N_B}\right)$$
Using x = (N_A - N_B)/N,
$$S = N k_B \ln 2 - \frac{N}{2} k_B \left[ (1 + x) \ln(1 + x) + (1 - x) \ln(1 - x) \right]$$

subquestions.subproblem: Compute the total interaction energy assuming that the atoms are randomly distributed among the sites.
subquestions.solution:
On average each atom has 6 nearest neighbors. For a random distribution, the interaction energy per atom with its six neighbors is
$$U = 6 \left[ -J \left( \frac{N_A}{N} \right)^2 - J \left( \frac{N_B}{N} \right)^2 + J \cdot 2 \frac{N_A}{N} \frac{N_B}{N} \right]$$
This simplifies to
$$U = - \frac{6 J}{N^2} (N_A - N_B)^2$$
Hence the total interaction energy is
$$E = \frac{N}{2} U$$
which gives
$$E = - \frac{3 J}{N} (N_A - N_B)^2$$
Using x = (N_A - N_B)/N,
$$E = - 3 N J x^2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E = ..., expressed solely in terms of N, J, and x (where x = (N_A - N_B)/N).

subquestions.subproblem: Compute the free energy of the system, F, as a function of x, where N_A = N(1 + x)/2 and N_B = N(1 - x)/2. Expand F(x) up to the 4th order in x. Show that there is a critical temperature T_c above and below which the curve F(x) has different characteristic shapes. Determine T_c and sketch F as a function of x for T > T_c, T = T_c and T < T_c.
subquestions.solution:
The free energy of the system is
$$F = E - T S$$
Using the results of parts (a) and (b) with N_A = N(1 + x)/2 and N_B = N(1 - x)/2, we obtain
$$F = - 3 N J x^2 - N k_B T \ln 2 + \frac{N k_B T x}{2} \ln \frac{1 + x}{1 - x} + \frac{N k_B T}{2} \ln(1 - x^2)$$
Using the series expansions
$$\ln(1 + x) = x - \frac{1}{2} x^2 + \frac{1}{3} x^3 - \frac{1}{4} x^4 + \cdots$$
$$\ln \frac{1 + x}{1 - x} = 2 \left( x + \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{x^5}{5} + \cdots \right)$$
the expansion of F(x) up to fourth order is
$$F = - N k_B T \ln 2 + \left( \frac{1}{2} N k_B T - 3 N J \right) x^2 + \frac{1}{12} N k_B T x^4 + \cdots$$
The critical temperature T_c satisfies
$$\frac{N}{2} k_B T_c - 3 N J = 0$$
$$T_c = \frac{6 J}{k_B}$$
At x = 0, the curvature conditions are:
$$(\frac{\partial^2 F}{\partial x^2})_{x=0} = 0$$
for T = T_c,
$$(\frac{\partial^2 F}{\partial x^2})_{x=0} > 0$$
for T > T_c, and
$$(\frac{\partial^2 F}{\partial x^2})_{x=0} < 0$$
for T < T_c, showing that T_c is the critical transition temperature. The compositions of the two separated phases are
$$x_1 = \sqrt{ \frac{3 ( T_c - T )}{T} }$$
$$x_2 = - \sqrt{ \frac{3 ( T_c - T )}{T} }$$

The conduction electrons are modeled as a free electron gas with scattering time tau and number density n. Let e be the elementary charge, m the electron mass, v the electron velocity, E the electric field, B the magnetic field, j the electric current density, D the electric displacement field, H the magnetic field intensity, P the polarization density, epsilon_0 the vacuum permittivity, mu_0 the vacuum permeability, c the speed of light, k the wave number, omega the angular frequency, and \hat z the unit vector along the z axis. The Kronecker delta is denoted by delta_{kl} and the Levi-Civita symbol by \varepsilon_{klq}. The Einstein summation convention over repeated spatial indices is used. Ohm's law is j = sigma E with conductivity sigma, and equivalently E = rho j with resistivity tensor rho. In part (b), vectors may be treated as column matrices when forming linear algebra relations, and we denote by R_mat the resistivity matrix mapping j to E, by A_mat the linear map from P to E, and by M_mat the linear map from j to E induced by the polarization current so that E = R_mat j and E = M_mat j. The speed of light c is defined by c = 1/sqrt(mu_0 epsilon_0).

subquestions.subproblem: Derive an expression for the resistivity tensor of this metal.
subquestions.solution:
In a scattering event for a conduction electron of momentum m v, the average change of momentum is m v. If on average it undergoes 1/tau scatterings per unit time, it experiences a damping force - m v/tau. Hence the electron equation of motion is
$$
m \frac{d v}{d t} = - e E - e v \times B - m \frac{v}{\tau}
$$
Using j = - n e v, this becomes
$$
- \frac{m}{n e} \frac{d j}{d t} = - e E + \frac{j \times B}{n} + \frac{m j}{\tau n e}
$$
Assume a time-harmonic solution
$$
j = j_0 e^{- i \omega t}
$$
Substitution gives
$$
E = \frac{m}{n e^2} \left( \frac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) j + \frac{j \times B}{n e}
$$
In components
$$
E_k = \frac{m}{n e^2} \left( \frac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) j_k + \frac{\varepsilon_{k l q} j_l B_q}{n e}
$$
Define the resistivity tensor by
$$
E_k = \rho_{k l} j_l
$$
with
$$
\rho_{k l} = \frac{m}{n e^2} \left( \frac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) \delta_{k l} + \frac{\varepsilon_{k l q} B_q}{n e}
$$
For B = B_0 \hat z, the tensor is
$$
\rho = \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{m}{n e^2} \left( \dfrac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) & \dfrac{B_0}{n e} & 0 \\
- \dfrac{B_0}{n e} & \dfrac{m}{n e^2} \left( \dfrac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \dfrac{m}{n e^2} \left( \dfrac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right)
\end{pmatrix}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be the resistivity tensor for B = B0 z-hat given as a 3x3 matrix ρ with entries written only in terms of m, n, e, τ, ω, and B0, ordered in the (x, y, z) basis. If you also provide a compact component form, it should be written as ρ_kl = (… ) using only m, n, e, τ, ω, B_q, δ_kl, and ε_klq.

subquestions.subproblem: Using the result of part (a), derive the low-frequency dispersion relation for electromagnetic waves propagating along \hat z in the metal.
subquestions.solution:
The constitutive relations are
$$
D = \epsilon_0 E + P
$$
$$
\nabla \cdot D = 0
$$
$$
B = \mu_0 H
$$
Maxwell's equations are
$$
\nabla \times E = - \frac{\partial B}{\partial t}
$$
$$
\nabla \times H = \frac{\partial D}{\partial t}
$$
Combining gives
$$
\mu_0 \frac{\partial^2 D}{\partial t^2} = \nabla^2 E - \nabla ( \nabla \cdot E )
$$
For a plane wave along \hat z write
$$
E = E_0 e^{i (k z - \omega t)}
$$
Then
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} = - i \omega
$$
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial z} = i k
$$
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial x} = 0
$$
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial y} = 0
$$
Substitution yields
$$
- \omega^2 \mu_0 ( \epsilon_0 E + P ) = - k^2 E + k^2 E_z \hat z
$$
From the divergence condition
$$
\nabla \cdot D = 0
$$
we have
$$
\frac{\partial D_z}{\partial z} = i k ( \epsilon_0 E_z + P_z )
$$
and
$$
i k ( \epsilon_0 E_z + P_z ) = 0
$$
Hence
$$
E_z = - \frac{P_z}{\epsilon_0}
$$
Therefore
$$
\left( k^2 - \frac{\omega^2}{c^2} \right) E = \mu_0 \omega^2 P - \frac{k^2}{\epsilon_0} P_z \hat z
$$
Define
$$
\chi = \left( \frac{c k}{\omega} \right)^2 - 1
$$
Then
$$
E = \frac{1}{\epsilon_0 \chi} \left[ P - ( \chi + 1 ) P_z \hat z \right]
$$
The polarization current density is
$$
j = \frac{d P}{d t}
$$
For the plane wave
$$
\frac{d P}{d t} = - i \omega P
$$
Write the linear relations with column vectors j, E, P and matrices R_mat, A_mat, M_mat
$$
E = R_{\text{mat}} j
$$
$$
E = A_{\text{mat}} P
$$
Using
$$
P = \frac{i}{\omega} j
$$
we have
$$
E = M_{\text{mat}} j
$$
with
$$
M_{\text{mat}} = \frac{i}{\omega} A_{\text{mat}}
$$
For a nontrivial j we require
$$
| R_{\text{mat}} - M_{\text{mat}} | = 0
$$
This leads to
$$
\left[ \frac{m}{n e^2} \left( \frac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) - \frac{i}{\epsilon_0 \chi \omega} \right]^2 = - \left( \frac{B_0}{n e} \right)^2
$$
Define the plasma frequency and cyclotron frequency by
$$
\omega_p = \sqrt{ \frac{n e^2}{\epsilon_0 m} }
$$
$$
\omega_c = \frac{e B_0}{m}
$$
Then
$$
\left[ \left( \frac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) - \frac{i \omega_p^2}{\chi \omega} \right]^2 = - \omega_c^2
$$
In the low-frequency limit with 1/\tau and \omega negligible compared to \omega_c we obtain
$$
- \frac{i \omega_p^2}{\chi \omega} = \pm i \omega_c
$$
Hence
$$
- \omega_p^2 = \pm \omega \omega_c \chi
$$
Using \chi = \frac{c^2 k^2}{\omega^2} - 1, the dispersion relations are
$$
\frac{c^2 k^2}{\omega^2} = 1 \mp \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega \omega_c}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single algebraic equation giving the low-frequency dispersion relation for propagation along z-hat, written explicitly as an expression for c^2 k^2 / ω^2 in terms of only the variables c, k, ω, ω_p, and ω_c.

subquestions.subproblem: derive the low-frequency dispersion relation for waves propagation along \hat z .Neglect \frac{1}{\tau} and \omega in comparison with the cyclotron frequency \omega_c .(Derive a wave equation for j ,the current density.)
subquestions.solution:
Start from the equation of motion and express it in terms of j using j = - n e v
$$
m \frac{d v}{d t} = - e E - e v \times B - m \frac{v}{\tau}
$$
$$
j = - n e v
$$
This gives
$$
\frac{d j}{d t} = \frac{n e^2}{m} E - \frac{1}{m} j \times B - \frac{j}{\tau}
$$
Assume plane-wave time dependence so that
$$
\frac{d j}{d t} = - i \omega j
$$
Using Maxwell's equations for fields proportional to e^{i (k z - \omega t)}
$$
\nabla \times E = - \frac{\partial B}{\partial t}
$$
$$
\nabla \times B = \mu_0 \epsilon_0 \frac{\partial E}{\partial t} + \mu_0 j
$$
Eliminating B gives
$$
\left( \frac{\omega^2}{c^2} - k^2 \right) E = i \mu_0 \omega j
$$
Equivalently
$$
E = - \frac{i}{\epsilon_0 \chi \omega} j
$$
with
$$
\chi = \left( \frac{c k}{\omega} \right)^2 - 1
$$
Insert this into the frequency-domain form of the equation of motion
$$
E = \frac{m}{n e^2} \left( \frac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) j + \frac{j \times B}{n e}
$$
For B = B_0 \hat z and propagation along \hat z, the transverse components satisfy
$$
\left[ \frac{i \mu_0 \omega}{\frac{\omega^2}{c^2} - k^2} - \frac{m}{n e^2} \left( \frac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) 
\right] j_x - \frac{B_0}{n e} j_y = 0
$$
$$
\frac{B_0}{n e} j_x + \left[ \frac{i \mu_0 \omega}{\frac{\omega^2}{c^2} - k^2} - \frac{m}{n e^2} \left( \frac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) 
\right] j_y = 0
$$
A nontrivial solution requires
$$
\left[ \frac{i \mu_0 \omega}{\frac{\omega^2}{c^2} - k^2} - \frac{m}{n e^2} \left( \frac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) \right]^2 = - \left( \frac{B_0}{n e} \right)^2
$$
Using \mu_0 c^2 = \frac{1}{\epsilon_0} and the definition of \chi, this is
$$
\left[ \frac{m}{n e^2} \left( \frac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) - \frac{i}{\epsilon_0 \chi \omega} \right]^2 = - \left( \frac{B_0}{n e} \right)^2
$$
Define
$$
\omega_p = \sqrt{ \frac{n e^2}{\epsilon_0 m} }
$$
$$
\omega_c = \frac{e B_0}{m}
$$
Then
$$
\left[ \left( \frac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) - \frac{i \omega_p^2}{\chi \omega} \right]^2 = - \omega_c^2
$$
In the low-frequency limit with 1/\tau and \omega negligible compared to \omega_c we obtain
$$
- \frac{i \omega_p^2}{\chi \omega} = \pm i \omega_c
$$
Hence
$$
- \omega_p^2 = \pm \omega \omega_c \chi
$$
Using \chi = \frac{c^2 k^2}{\omega^2} - 1, the dispersion relations are
$$
\frac{c^2 k^2}{\omega^2} = 1 \mp \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega \omega_c}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single algebraic equation for the low-frequency dispersion relation along z-hat obtained via a wave equation for j, written explicitly as an expression for c^2 k^2 / ω^2 using only the variables c, k, ω, ω_p, and ω_c.

grading_standard.formula: $$m \frac{d v}{d t} = - e E - e v \times B - m \frac{v}{\tau}$$
$$- \frac{m}{n e} \frac{d j}{d t} = - e E + \frac{j \times B}{n} + \frac{m j}{\tau n e}$$
$$E_k = \frac{m}{n e^2} \left( \frac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) j_k + \frac{\varepsilon_{k l q} j_l B_q}{n e}$$
$$\rho_{k l} = \frac{m}{n e^2} \left( \frac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) \delta_{k l} + \frac{\varepsilon_{k l q} B_q}{n e}$$

$$\rho = \begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{m}{n e^2} \left( \dfrac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) & \dfrac{B_0}{n e} & 0 \\
- \dfrac{B_0}{n e} & \dfrac{m}{n e^2} \left( \dfrac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right) & 0 \\
0 & 0 & \dfrac{m}{n e^2} \left( \dfrac{1}{\tau} - i \omega \right)
\end{pmatrix}$$
$$- \omega^2 \mu_0 ( \epsilon_0 E + P ) = - k^2 E + k^2 E_z \hat z$$
$$\frac{\partial D_z}{\partial z} = i k ( \epsilon_0 E_z + P_z )$$

subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the estimated values of ω_p and ω_0 as numerical values in s^{-1}. Report both values with 2 significant figures and include units.

subquestions.subproblem: At room temperature, calculate \sigma(\omega), the complex frequency-dependent conductivity of Cu.
subquestions.solution:
Ohm's law gives $$
J=\sigma E
$$ The polarization current density is $$
J=\frac{dP}{dt}
$$ and $$
\frac{dP}{dt}=-i\omega P
$$ The electric susceptibility is $$
\chi=\frac{P}{\epsilon_0 E}
$$ so $$
\chi=\frac{i\sigma}{\epsilon_0\omega}
$$ The electric displacement satisfies $$
D=\varepsilon E
$$ and $$
D=\epsilon_0 E+P
$$ which yields $$
\varepsilon(\omega)=1+\chi
$$ $$
\varepsilon(\omega)=1+\frac{i\sigma(\omega)}{\epsilon_0\omega}
$$ Using the Drude-Lorentz form for \varepsilon(\omega), $$
\frac{i\sigma}{\epsilon_0\omega}=\frac{\omega_p^2}{(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)-i\omega\tau^{-1}}
$$ Solving for \sigma(\omega) gives $$
\sigma(\omega)=\frac{\epsilon_0\omega\omega_p^2\big[\omega\tau^{-1}-i(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)\big]}{(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\omega^2\tau^{-2}}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of σ(ω) = ..., expressed solely in terms of ε_0, ω, ω_p, ω_0, τ, and i.

subquestions.subproblem: What is \sigma(\omega) for perfectly pure, defect-free Cu at zero temperature?
subquestions.solution:
At zero temperature, $$
\tau\to\infty
$$ the conductivity is $$
\sigma(\omega)=-\frac{i\epsilon_0\omega\omega_p^2}{\omega_0^2-\omega^2}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of σ(ω) = ..., expressed solely in terms of ε_0, ω, ω_p, ω_0, and i.

context: At time t=0 a charge density distribution ρ(r) exists within an idealized homogeneous and isotropic conductor whose permittivity ε and conductivity σ are constants, independent of position and time. Let r denote the position vector and t the time. Let E be the electric field, D the electric displacement field, and j the conduction current density. Using Maxwell's equations and Ohm's law, find the charge density ρ(r,t) for subsequent times t>0, given the initial condition ρ(r,0)=ρ(r).
solution:
From Gauss's law for electricity
$$
\nabla \cdot D = \rho
$$

With the constitutive relation in a homogeneous medium
$$
D = \epsilon E
$$

Ohm's law for a conductor is
$$
j = \sigma E
$$

Charge conservation (continuity equation) gives
$$
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot j = 0
$$

From Gauss's law and the constitutive relation
$$
\nabla \cdot E = \frac{\rho}{\epsilon}
$$

Therefore
$$
\nabla \cdot j = \sigma \nabla \cdot E
$$

Hence
$$
\nabla \cdot j = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon} \rho
$$

Substituting into the continuity equation yields
$$
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon} \rho = 0
$$

With the initial condition
$$
\rho(r,0) = \rho(r)
$$

the solution is
$$
\rho(r,t) = \rho(r) e^{-\sigma t / \epsilon}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \rho(r,t) = ..., and your response should be written with \rho(r), \sigma, \epsilon, and t.

context: Consider a two-dimensional square lattice of lattice constant a. Its first Brillouin zone is a square of edge length 2 pi over a in reciprocal space, as in Fig. 1.16. Let b_1 and b_2 denote the primitive reciprocal lattice vectors along x and y, each of magnitude 2 pi over a. Let vector wavevectors be denoted by \vec{k} and their magnitudes by k = |\vec{k}|. Let m be the electron mass and hbar the reduced Planck constant. Let p be the crystal momentum, with p = hbar k. Let X denote the midpoint of a zone edge, for example \vec{k}_X = (pi over a, 0), and let M denote a zone corner, for example \vec{k}_M = (pi over a, pi over a). Define E_X and E_M as the free-electron kinetic energies at X and M, respectively. In part a, the factor b is defined by b = E_M divided by E_X. The crystal potential is V(x,y), with V_0 a constant amplitude, and V_G denotes the Fourier coefficient of V at reciprocal lattice vector G. Let Delta_x be the energy gap at X. In part c, assume the material is divalent, meaning that the lowest band is completely filled at zero temperature if a band gap exists, and the system is metallic if the lowest two bands overlap in energy.

subquestions.subproblem: The kinetic energy of a free electron at a corner of the first Brillouin zone is larger than that of an electron at the midpoint of a side face of the zone by a factor b. Calculate b.
subquestions.solution:
The free-electron kinetic energy is
$$E=\frac{p^2}{2m}$$
with
$$p=\hbar k$$
thus
$$E=\frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2m}$$
At the midpoint X, the wavevector is
$$\vec{k}_X=\left(\frac{\pi}{a},0\right)$$
so its magnitude is
$$k_X=\frac{\pi}{a}$$
and the energy is
$$E_X=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\left(\frac{\pi}{a}\right)^2$$
At the corner M, the wavevector is
$$\vec{k}_M=\left(\frac{\pi}{a},\frac{\pi}{a}\right)$$
so its magnitude is
$$k_M=\sqrt{2}\frac{\pi}{a}$$
and the energy is
$$E_M=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\,2\left(\frac{\pi}{a}\right)^2$$
The required factor is
$$b=\frac{E_M}{E_X}$$
thus
$$b=2$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express b as a numerical value with 1 significant figure.

subquestions.subproblem: The crystal potential of the corresponding material is V(x,y) = -2 V_0 (cos(2 pi x over a) + cos(2 pi y over a)), where V_0 is a constant and a is the lattice spacing. Find approximately the energy gap at the midpoint of the zone face.
subquestions.solution:
Write the potential in Fourier form
$$V(x,y)=-V_0\left(e^{i2\pi x/a}+e^{-i2\pi x/a}+e^{i2\pi y/a}+e^{-i2\pi y/a}\right)$$
For G = (\pm 2\pi/a,0) and G = (0,\pm 2\pi/a), the Fourier coefficient is
$$V_G=-V_0$$
At the midpoint X, the gap in the nearly free electron approximation is
$$\Delta_x=2\lvert V_G\rvert$$
Therefore
$$\Delta_x=2\lvert V_0\rvert$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form \Delta_x = ..., and your response should be written with V_0 only.

subquestions.subproblem: Assuming that your result in part b is exact and that the material is divalent, write down a condition for the system to be metallic.
subquestions.solution:
For a divalent material, metallic behavior requires band overlap
$$E_X+\Delta_x\leq E_M$$
Using
$$E_X=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\left(\frac{\pi}{a}\right)^2$$
and
$$E_M=\frac{\hbar^2}{m}\left(\frac{\pi}{a}\right)^2$$
with
$$\Delta_x=2\lvert V_0\rvert$$
the condition becomes
$$\lvert V_0\rvert\leq\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{4ma^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as a single inequality of the form (condition) involving only V_0, \hbar, m, and a.

context: Consider an intrinsic semiconductor whose electronic density of states function N(E) is depicted in Fig. 1.23. Definitions and notation: E is the electron energy. N(E) is the electronic density of states per unit volume per unit energy and already includes the spin degeneracy factor of 2. E_c is the conduction-band minimum. E_v is the valence-band maximum. E_F is the Fermi level. f(E) is the Fermi-Dirac distribution function. n is the density of conduction-band electrons. p is the density of valence-band holes. k_B is the Boltzmann constant. T is the absolute temperature. E_g = E_c - E_v is the band gap energy. n_0 denotes an effective constant density-of-states factor near the relevant band edge as suggested by the figure. Assume the nondegenerate (Boltzmann) limit in the bands, i.e., E - E_F \gg k_B T where used. For the numerical estimate at room temperature, use E_c - E_F \approx E_g/2 = 0.75 \unit{eV} and k_B T = \frac{1}{40} \unit{eV}. Tasks: (1) Locate the Fermi level with respect to the valence and conduction bands for an intrinsic semiconductor. (2) Write the Fermi-Dirac distribution function f(E). (3) Estimate the density of conduction-band electrons at room temperature.
solution:
(1) The conduction-band electron density n and valence-band hole density p are given by
$$
n = \int_{E_c}^{\infty} N(E) f(E) dE
$$
$$
p = \int_{-\infty}^{E_v} N(E) \bigl(1 - f(E)\bigr) dE
$$
For the nondegenerate limit in the bands we use
$$
f(E) \approx e^{-\frac{E - E_F}{k_B T}}
$$
Approximating the density of states near the relevant band edge by a constant n_0 gives
$$
n \approx \int_{E_c}^{\infty} n_0 e^{-\frac{E - E_F}{k_B T}} dE
$$
$$
n \approx n_0 k_B T e^{-\frac{E_c - E_F}{k_B T}}
$$
$$
p \approx n_0 k_B T e^{-\frac{E_F - E_v}{k_B T}}
$$
For an intrinsic semiconductor n = p, hence
$$
n = p
$$
$$
E_F = \frac{E_c + E_v}{2}
$$
(2) The Fermi-Dirac distribution function is
$$
f(E) = \frac{1}{e^{\frac{E - E_F}{k_B T}} + 1}
$$
(3) Using the given room-temperature values
$$
E_c - E_F \approx \frac{E_g}{2}
$$
$$
\frac{E_g}{2} = 0.75 \unit{eV}
$$
$$
k_B T = \frac{1}{40} \unit{eV}
$$
The conduction-band electron density is
$$
n \approx n_0 k_B T \exp\biggl(-\frac{E_c - E_F}{k_B T}\biggr)
$$
$$
n \approx 4.68 \times 10^6 \unit{cm^{-3}}
$$

subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E_F = ..., and your response should be written with E_c, E_v.
Your final answer should be given in the form of f(E) = ..., and your response should be written with E, E_F, k_B, T.
Your final answer should express the conduction-band electron density n at room temperature as a numerical value in cm^-3. Report the result to three significant figures.

$$p \approx n_0 k_B T e^{-\frac{E_F - E_v}{k_B T}}$$

context: At room temperature, with Boltzmann constant k_B, temperature T, and elementary charge e, the thermal voltage satisfies k_B T / e = 26 mV. A sample of cadmium sulfide (CdS) has mobile carrier density n = 10^16 cm^{-3} and mobility coefficient mu = 10^2 cm^2 V^{-1} s^{-1}. Let sigma denote the electrical conductivity, l the root-mean-square distance a carrier diffuses between successive trappings, t the average free lifetime in a mobile state, m the mass of a free electron, and m* the effective mass of a carrier. Use e for the magnitude of the electron charge.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the electrical conductivity sigma of this sample.
subquestions.solution:
The electrical conductivity is given by
$$
\sigma = n e mu
$$
The given carrier density is
$$
n = 10^{16} \unit{cm^{-3}}
$$
Converting to SI units gives
$$
n = 10^{22} \unit{m^{-3}}
$$
The elementary charge is
$$
e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \unit{C}
$$
The mobility in SI units is
$$
mu = 10^{-2} \unit{m^2 V^{-1} s^{-1}}
$$
Therefore
$$
\sigma = 16 \unit{\Omega^{-1} m^{-1}}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the electrical conductivity sigma as a numerical value in SI units (Ω^{-1} m^{-1}), rounded to 2 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: The carriers are continuously trapped into immobile sites and then thermally reionized into mobile states. If the average free lifetime in a mobile state is t = 10^{-5} s, what is the rms distance l a carrier diffuses between successive trappings?
subquestions.solution:
Equipartition gives for each Cartesian component
$$
\frac{1}{2} m \bar v_x^2 = \frac{1}{2} k_B T
$$
Similarly for y and z, so for three degrees of freedom
$$
\frac{1}{2} m \bar v^2 = \frac{3}{2} k_B T
$$
Hence
$$
\bar v^2 = \frac{3 k_B T}{m}
$$
The rms distance between trappings is
$$
l^2 = \bar v^2 t^2
$$
Thus
$$
l = \sqrt{\frac{3 k_B T}{m}}\, t
$$
Using the given thermal voltage and charge-to-mass ratio
$$
\frac{k_B T}{e} = 26 \unit{mV}
$$
$$
\frac{e}{m} = 1.76 \times 10^{11} \unit{C kg^{-1}}
$$
One may write
$$
l = \sqrt{3 \left( \frac{k_B T}{e} \right) \left( \frac{e}{m} \right)}\, t
$$
With
$$
t = 10^{-5} \unit{s}
$$
we obtain
$$
l = 1.17 \unit{m}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the rms distance l as a numerical value in SI units (m), rounded to 3 significant figures.

subquestions.subproblem: If the charge carriers have an effective mass m* equal to 1/10 times the mass m of a free electron, what is the average time ⟨τ⟩ between successive scatterings?
subquestions.solution:
In the Drude model
$$
\sigma = \frac{n e^2 \langle \tau \rangle}{m^*}
$$
Thus
$$
\langle \tau \rangle = \frac{m^* \sigma}{n e^2}
$$
With
$$
m^* = \frac{1}{10} m
$$
$$
\sigma = 16 \unit{\Omega^{-1} m^{-1}}
$$
$$
n = 10^{22} \unit{m^{-3}}
$$
$$

solution:
The differential cross section for Rutherford scattering of a carrier of charge e, mass m, and speed v by an impurity nucleus of charge Ze per unit solid angle is

$$
\frac{d\sigma_{sc}}{d\Omega}=R^2 \csc^4\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)
$$

$$
R=\frac{Z e^2}{8 \pi \epsilon m v^2}
$$

The transport cross section is

$$
\sigma_{tr}=\int (1-\cos \theta) \frac{d\sigma_{sc}}{d\Omega} d\Omega
$$

Define the dimensionless angular factor A_\Omega by

$$
\sigma_{tr}=A_\Omega R^2
$$

The scattering rate is

$$
\frac{1}{\tau}=n_i v \sigma_{tr}
$$

Substituting \sigma_{tr} gives

$$
\frac{1}{\tau}=n_i v A_\Omega R^2
$$

Using R from above yields

$$
\frac{1}{\tau}=\frac{n_i A_\Omega Z^2 e^4}{64 \pi^2 \epsilon^2 m^2} \frac{1}{v^3}
$$

Hence

$$
\tau=\frac{64 \pi^2 \epsilon^2 m^2}{n_i A_\Omega Z^2 e^4} v^3
$$

For nondegenerate carriers with Maxwellian statistics, use the thermal speed

$$
v_{th}=\sqrt{\frac{8 k_B T}{\pi m}}
$$

Therefore

$$
\tau(T)=\frac{64 \pi^2 \epsilon^2 m^2}{n_i A_\Omega Z^2 e^4} v_{th}^3
$$

The conductivity is

$$
\sigma=\frac{n e^2 \tau}{m}
$$

Thus

$$
\sigma(T)=\frac{n e^2}{m} \tau(T)
$$

Therefore the temperature dependence has the form

$$
\sigma(T)=C T^{\frac{3}{2}}
$$

with

$$
C=\frac{n e^2}{m} \frac{64 \pi^2 \epsilon^2 m^2}{n_i A_\Omega Z^2 e^4} \left(\frac{8 k_B}{\pi m}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}
$$

context: Derive an expression for the Hall coefficient for an intrinsic semiconductor in terms of the electron and hole mobilities and the carrier density. Consider a rectangular sample lying in the xy-plane with an applied electric field E_x along +x and a uniform magnetic field B_z along +z. Electrons (density n, mobility mu_n) and holes (density p, mobility mu_p) drift under E_x with drift velocities v_{n,x} and v_{p,x}, respectively. By definition, for holes v_{p,x}=mu_p E_x, while for electrons the drift is opposite to the field so v_{n,x}=-mu_n E_x. The Lorentz force q v × B deflects both carrier types along -y, producing a transverse Hall electric field epsilon_y such that the net current density along y vanishes in steady state. The partial current densities along y are denoted (J_p)_y and (J_n)_y, and the total current densities are J_y along y and J_x along x. The conductivity is sigma and the elementary charge magnitude is q>0. The Hall coefficient R_H is defined by R_H=epsilon_y/(J_x B_z).
solution:
The conductivity of the semiconductor is
$$
\sigma = n q \mu_n + p q \mu_p
$$
The hole current density along y is
$$
(J_p)_y = p q \mu_p \varepsilon_y - p q \mu_p v_{p,x} B_z
$$
Using v_{p,x}=\mu_p E_x gives
$$
(J_p)_y = p q \mu_p \varepsilon_y - p q \mu_p^2 E_x B_z
$$
The electron current density along y is
$$
(J_n)_y = n q \mu_n \varepsilon_y - n q \mu_n v_{n,x} B_z
$$
Using v_{n,x}=-\mu_n E_x gives
$$
(J_n)_y = n q \mu_n \varepsilon_y + n q \mu_n^2 E_x B_z
$$
In steady state the net y current vanishes
$$
J_y = (J_p)_y + (J_n)_y
$$
$$
J_y = 0
$$
Solving for the Hall field yields
$$
\varepsilon_y = \frac{p \mu_p^2 - n \mu_n^2}{p \mu_p + n \mu_n} E_x B_z
$$
Along x we have
$$
J_x = \sigma E_x
$$
The Hall coefficient, defined by R_H = \varepsilon_y/(J_x B_z), is then
$$
R_H = \frac{1}{q} \frac{p \mu_p^2 - n \mu_n^2}{(p \mu_p + n \mu_n)^2}
$$
For an intrinsic semiconductor the carrier densities are equal
$$
n = p
$$
Hence
$$
R_H = \frac{1}{q n} \frac{\mu_p - \mu_n}{\mu_p + \mu_n}
$$

populations are $$N_+=\int_0^{E_+}\rho(E)\,dE$$ $$N_-=\int_0^{E_-}\rho(E)\,dE$$ At T=0 the common Fermi level satisfies $$\varepsilon_0=E_+-\mu_B B$$ $$\varepsilon_0=E_-+\mu_B B$$ Hence $$E_+=\varepsilon_0+\mu_B B$$ $$E_-=\varepsilon_0-\mu_B B$$ Using N_+=(1/2)N(1+x) and N_-=(1/2)N(1-x), we obtain $$N_+=\frac{2}{3}C\left(\varepsilon_0+\mu_B B\right)^{3/2}$$ $$N_-=\frac{2}{3}C\left(\varepsilon_0-\mu_B B\right)^{3/2}$$ At zero field, the total number fixes C via $$N=2\int_0^{E_F}\rho(E)\,dE$$ $$N=\frac{4}{3}C E_F^{3/2}$$ Thus $$C=\frac{3}{4}N E_F^{-3/2}$$ Using these relations, one finds $$\varepsilon_0+\mu_B B=E_F(1+x)^{2/3}$$ $$\varepsilon_0-\mu_B B=E_F(1-x)^{2/3}$$ For x\ll 1, their difference gives $$x\approx\frac{3\mu_B B}{2E_F}$$ The total energy of the spin-up subsystem is $$E_{+\,\mathrm{tot}}=\int_0^{\varepsilon_0+\mu_B B}(E-\mu_B B)\rho(E)\,dE$$ $$E_{+\,\mathrm{tot}}=\frac{2}{5}C\left(\varepsilon_0+\mu_B B\right)^{5/2}-\mu_B B N_+$$ $$E_{+\,\mathrm{tot}}=\frac{3}{10}E_F N(1+x)^{5/3}-\frac{1}{2}\mu_B B N(1+x)$$ The total energy of the spin-down subsystem is $$E_{-\,\mathrm{tot}}=\int_0^{\varepsilon_0-\mu_B B}(E+\mu_B B)\rho(E)\,dE$$ $$E_{-\,\mathrm{tot}}=\frac{2}{5}C\left(\varepsilon_0-\mu_B B\right)^{5/2}+\mu_B B N_-$$ $$E_{-\,\mathrm{tot}}=\frac{3}{10}E_F N(1-x)^{5/3}+\frac{1}{2}\mu_B B N(1-x)$$ Therefore the total energy is $$E_{\mathrm{tot}}=\frac{3}{10}N E_F\left[(1+x)^{5/3}+(1-x)^{5/3}\right]-\mu_B B N x$$ For x\ll 1, this gives $$E_{\mathrm{tot}}\approx\frac{3}{5}N E_F-\mu_B B N x$$ Using the relation for x yields $$E_{\mathrm{tot}}\approx\frac{3}{5}N E_F-\frac{2\mu_B^2 B^2}{2E_F}N$$ The total magnetic moment is $$vM=(N_+-N_-)\mu_B$$ Hence $$vM=N x\mu_B$$ and the magnetization is $$M=n x\mu_B$$ Using the small-field result for x yields $$M=\frac{3 n\mu_B^2 B}{2E_F}$$

subquestions.subproblem: We may approximate the effect of exchange interactions among the conduction electrons if we assume that only electrons with parallel spins interact with each other, with energy −V per pair where V>0. How is the magnetization modified?
subquestions.solution: The number of parallel-spin pairs among N_+ electrons is approximately $$\frac{1}{2}N_+^2$$ Each pair contributes energy −V, so the spin-up energy including interactions is $$E_{+\,\mathrm{tot}}\approx\frac{3}{10}E_F N(1+x)^{5/3}-\frac{1}{2}\mu_B B N(1+x)-\frac{1}{8}V N^2(1+x)^2$$ Similarly, for spin down $$E_{-\,\mathrm{tot}}\approx\frac{3}{10}E_F N(1-x)^{5/3}+\frac{1}{2}\mu_B B N(1-x)-\frac{1}{8}V N^2(1-x)^2$$ The total energy is $$E_{\mathrm{tot}}=\frac{3}{10}E_F N\left[(1+x)^{5/3}+(1-x)^{5/3}\right]-\mu_B B N x-\frac{V}{8}N^2\left[(1+x)^2+(1-x)^2\right]$$ At equilibrium, dE_{tot}/dx=0 gives $$\frac{1}{2}E_F\left[(1+x)^{2/3}-(1-x)^{2/3}\right]-\mu_B B-\frac{V}{4}N\left[(1+x)-(1-x)\right]=0$$ For x\ll 1, this yields $$x\approx\frac{6\mu_B B}{4E_F-3 V N}$$ Hence the magnetization is $$M=n x\mu_B$$ $$M=\frac{6 n\mu_B^2 B}{4E_F-3 V N}$$ For V=0 this reduces to the non-interacting result
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as a single explicit algebraic expression for the magnetization in the form M = [an expression in n, μ_B, B, E_F, V, N]. Do not introduce any additional variables.

context: Consider an ideal gas of non-interacting, stable vector mesons (massive particles with spin 1) with magnetic moment μ in a uniform magnetic field. Let B denote the magnetic flux density, H the magnetic field strength, and μ_0 the vacuum permeability, related by B=μ_0 H in SI units. Let k_B be the Boltzmann constant, T the absolute temperature, β=1/(k_B T), and n the number of particles per unit volume. Let M be the magnetization per unit volume and χ the paramagnetic susceptibility per unit volume, defined by χ=M/H. In part (a), treat the three spin projections m=+1,0,−1 with Zeeman energies −μ B m. In part (b), treat a classical magnetic dipole of fixed magnitude μ making an angle θ with B.

subquestions.subproblem: Compute the paramagnetic susceptibility per unit volume in a weak magnetic field.
subquestions.solution:
For a single spin-1 particle with Zeeman energies −μ B m for m=+1,0,−1, the single-particle partition function over spin states is
$$z_1=e^{-\beta \varepsilon}+1+e^{\beta \varepsilon}$$
with
$$\varepsilon=\mu B$$
and
$$\beta=\frac{1}{k_B T}$$
The probabilities for its magnetic moment to be parallel, perpendicular, and antiparallel to B are
$$P_+=\frac{e^{\beta \varepsilon}}{z_1}$$
$$P_0=\frac{1}{z_1}$$
$$P_-=\frac{e^{-\beta \varepsilon}}{z_1}$$
The mean magnetic moment along B per particle is
$$\bar{\mu}=\mu\left(P_+-P_-\right)$$
$$\bar{\mu}=\frac{2\mu\sinh(\beta \varepsilon)}{2\cosh(\beta \varepsilon)+1}$$
Thus the magnetization per unit volume is
$$M=n\bar{\mu}$$
$$M=\frac{2n\mu\sinh(\beta \varepsilon)}{2\cosh(\beta \varepsilon)+1}$$
In a weak magnetic field,
$$\mu B\ll k_B T$$
and
$$\beta \varepsilon\ll 1$$
with the approximations
$$\sinh(\beta \varepsilon)\approx \beta \varepsilon$$
$$\cosh(\beta \varepsilon)\approx 1$$
This gives
$$M=\frac{2n\mu\beta \varepsilon}{3}$$
$$M=\frac{2n\mu^2 B}{3k_B T}$$
The susceptibility is
$$\chi=\frac{M}{H}$$
Using B=\mu_0 H,
$$\chi=\frac{\mu_0 M}{B}$$
Therefore,
$$\chi=\frac{2n\mu_0 \mu^2}{3k_B T}$$

subquestions.subproblem: Perform the corresponding calculation with classical dipoles.
subquestions.solution:
For a classical magnetic dipole of fixed magnitude μ, the potential energy in a magnetic field B at polar angle θ is
$$\varepsilon=-\mu B\cos\theta$$
The Boltzmann weight is
$$e^{-\varepsilon/(k_B T)}=e^{\beta \mu B\cos\theta}$$
The mean magnetic moment along B is
$$\bar{\mu}=\frac{\int_0^{\pi} \mu \cos\theta\, e^{\beta \mu B\cos\theta}\, 2\pi \sin\theta\, d\theta}{\int_0^{\pi} e^{\beta \mu B\cos\theta}\, 2\pi \sin\theta\, d\theta}$$
Evaluating the integrals gives
$$\bar{\mu}=\mu\left[\coth(\mu B\beta)-\frac{1}{\mu B\beta}\right]$$
For a weak field,
$$\mu B\ll \frac{1}{\beta}$$
and
$$\mu B\beta\ll 1$$
with the expansion
$$\coth(\mu B\beta)\approx \frac{1}{\mu B\beta}+\frac{\mu B\beta}{3}$$
Thus the magnetization per unit volume is
$$M=n\bar{\mu}$$
$$M\approx \frac{n\mu^2 B\beta}{3}$$
The susceptibility is
$$\chi=\frac{M}{H}$$
Using B=\mu_0 H,
$$\chi=\frac{\mu_0 M}{B}$$
Therefore,
$$\chi=\frac{n\mu_0 \mu^2}{3k_B T}$$
